case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.limits: Sullivan protects against liability without fault, not against negligence claims by private figures, and it never contemplated a speaker with no mental state at all. Whether recklessness can be measured on a system that was warned its outputs err is the open question plaintiffs are building toward.
case.holding: A public official cannot recover for defamation without proving actual malice, knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard for the truth, a constitutional floor under every American defamation claim.
case.case_name: New York Times Co. v. Sullivan
case.why_ai_cites_it: The fault standard is where AI defamation claims go to die. When a model hallucinates about a public figure, the provider argues no human knew the statement was false and no one recklessly disregarded a truth they never saw, and the first decided chatbot-defamation case was won on exactly that ground.

reading.body:
New York Times v. Sullivan, the 1964 case requiring proof of actual malice for a public official's defamation claim, is described here as where AI defamation claims go to die, and it is quoted twice in X.AI v. Ellison filings and cited in defense across the four Character Technologies cases in this collection.

The record notes that the first decided chatbot-defamation case was won on exactly this ground, no human knew a hallucinated statement was false and no one recklessly disregarded a truth they never saw, which makes this the one precedent in this collection with a stated outcome already attached to it rather than an open question.

The case's own limit is where the next fight is heading. Sullivan protects against liability without fault, not negligence claims by private figures, and it never contemplated a speaker with no mental state at all, which the data flags as the open question plaintiffs are building toward rather than one already resolved.
